question: Broadly shared: do multimodal non-pharmacological programmes (physical plus cognitive activity, with or without risk-factor care) improve cognition in older adults with MCI? The channel (cognitive test outcomes) matches. But P-914 is a narrative review whose claim is hedged and set against single-domain approaches, and it leans on FINGER, which enrolled at-risk adults with normal-range cognition. P-895 is one trial of a 12-week Tai Chi plus group cognitive-leisure programme with quarterly nurse visits, compared with nurse-led risk-factor modification alone and with health-advice pamphlets.
metric: Mismatch: P-895 reports between-group differences in ADAS-Cog Z score with 95% CIs. P-914 reports no effect estimate of any kind (narrative synthesis, no pooling), only a qualitative statement that combinations 'may yield additive or synergistic benefits'.

figures.P-895: ADAS-Cog Z at 15 months (primary, modified ITT, Bonferroni): CPR vs health advice beta -0.04 (95% CI -0.34 to 0.26); RFM vs health advice -0.14 (-0.44 to 0.15); CPR vs RFM 0.10 (-0.19 to 0.40); also null at 6 and 12 months. Attendance 59% of Tai Chi and 58% of cognitive sessions.
figures.P-914: No estimate. The narrative claim: combined social, cognitive and physical stimulation 'may yield additive or synergistic benefits' in MCI. The same review states that several RCTs, especially short-duration or low-intensity programmes, found modest or non-significant effects. No interval can be derived because there is no estimate and no evaluation set.

matched_figure_check: None possible. P-914 has no quantitative figure under any condition. At claim level, P-914's own caveat covers P-895's situation, which its authors describe as a short 3-month active phase with low compliance.
reason: P-914 reports no effect size, so there is no second estimate whose interval P-895's could exclude, and conditions 2 and 4 cannot be met. The record hardens P-914's hedged 'may yield additive or synergistic benefits' into 'produce' and omits P-914's own statement that short or low-intensity trials often show non-significant results. P-895's authors place their trial in exactly that category (12-week active phase, about 58% attendance). Read as printed, the two papers do not disagree.

quotes.quote: No significant difference between the three groups in ADAS-Cog was found at the primary endpoint at 15 months (CPR vs health advice, β= –0⋅04 [95% CI –0⋅34 to 0⋅26]; RFM vs health advice, β= –0⋅14 [–0⋅44 to 0⋅15]; CPR vs RFM, β=0⋅10 [–0⋅19 to 0⋅40]) nor at the 6-month and 12-month follow-ups.
In the CPR group, participants attended a mean of 59% (36) of the 36 Tai Chi sessions and 58% (37) of the 36 cognitive sessions.
the relatively short intervention period of 3 months and low compliance with the intervention might have affected the study results.

emerging evidence suggests that combining social, cognitive, and physical stimulation into integrated multimodal interventions may yield additive or synergistic benefits for cognitive health in older adults with MCI.

Notably, not all interventions have yielded positive outcomes. Several randomized controlled trials have reported modest or non-significant cognitive improvements, especially in short-duration or low-intensity programs
We acknowledge that narrative synthesis may introduce selection bias
